title: Circular Seating Arrangement: Round Tables and Complex Puzzles

questions.question: For a person facing the centre of a circular table, which direction does their LEFT run as seen from above?
questions.rationale: Facing the centre, a person's left hand points anti-clockwise around the ring and their right points clockwise, as seen from above. Facing outward reverses both directions.

questions.question: How does the left-right convention change when everyone faces outward?
options: Left becomes clockwise and right becomes anti-clockwise
Left and right stay the same
Left and right both point to the centre
Outward-facing people have no left or right
questions.rationale: Facing outward is the reverse of facing the centre: the person's left runs clockwise and their right runs anti-clockwise. Every directional clue must be re-read through the sitter's own facing.

questions.question: Why should you fix one person at a chosen seat before doing anything else?
options: Because that person is always the most important
To break the rotational symmetry of the circle
To reduce the number of seats by one
Because opposite pairs depend on it
questions.rationale: A circle can be spun without changing any clue, so every rotation is equally valid. Fixing one person's seat destroys this rotational symmetry and turns the puzzle into a fixed sequence of seats.

questions.question: In the worked example, the final clockwise order from B is B, C, A, H, G, E, D, F. Who sits opposite B?
questions.rationale: With eight seats, the person opposite sits four away. From B at seat 1, counting four seats clockwise gives seat 5, which is occupied by G.

questions.question: In that same arrangement, who are A's immediate neighbours?
questions.rationale: A sits at seat 3, with C at seat 2 and H at seat 4 on either side, so A's immediate neighbours are C and H.

questions.question: The clue 'A sits second to the right of B' (both facing the centre) is resolved how?
options: Count two seats anti-clockwise from B
Count two seats clockwise from B
Count two seats upward from B
questions.rationale: Centre-facing right means clockwise, so counting starts at B's clockwise neighbour and stops at the second seat clockwise from B — in the worked example, seat 3.

questions.question: Why are 'opposite' clues best placed first in an even-count circle?
options: They fix two seats four apart in one step
They are the only definite clues possible
Odd circles have no opposites either
questions.rationale: An 'opposite' clue locks two seats at once, four positions apart in an even-count circle, giving two anchors immediately — the strongest opening move available.

questions.question: In a circle with seven seats, what happens to 'opposite' clues?
options: Nobody sits exactly opposite anyone — do not hunt for opposite pairs
They only apply to corner seats
questions.rationale: Opposite requires a seat exactly half-way around the ring. With an odd count such as seven, no seat is exactly opposite another, so opposite clues cannot exist — a classic trap.

questions.question: In the worked example, who sits third to the right of E (seat 6, everyone facing the centre)?
questions.rationale: Right is clockwise: from seat 6, the first seat clockwise is 7 (D), then 8 (F), then 1 (B) — remembering that the ring wraps across the top of the seat numbering.

questions.question: How do floor-based puzzles relate to circular seating, according to the lesson?
options: They use the same engine: definite, relative, and negative clues in the same order
They can only be solved after the circle is complete
questions.rationale: Eight people on four floors use the same deduction engine: 'A lives on floor 3' is definite, 'A lives above B' is relative, and 'C does not live on floor 1' is negative — the definite-relative-negative order still rules.
